citations.quote: For any field $k$, the category of strong symmetric monoidal functors $\mathsf{Cob}^{\mathrm{cl}}_2\to\mathrm{Vect}_{\mathrm{fd}}(k)$ and monoidal natural transformations is equivalent to the category of finite-dimensional commutative Frobenius $k$-algebras and maps preserving multiplication, unit, comultiplication, and counit.

If $M$ is connected with genus $g$, $m$ incoming circles and $n$ outgoing circles, its value under the functor corresponding to $(C,\mu,\eta,\Delta,\epsilon)$ is $$ \Delta_C^{[n]}\circ H^g\circ\mu_C^{[m]}:C^{\otimes m}\to C^{\otimes n}, \qquad H:=\mu_C\Delta_C, $$

derivations.claim: Coordinatewise multiplication is associative and commutative, and $1_A=\sum_i e_i$ is a unit because $e_i1_A=e_i$. The pairing matrix is $\operatorname{diag}(w_1,\ldots,w_r)$, whose determinant $\prod_i w_i$ is nonzero since every $w_i\ne0$; hence $b(a,b)=\epsilon(ab)$ is nondegenerate.

The formulas for $\Delta$ and $\epsilon$ are linear maps. For each $i$, both counit composites give $w_i^{-1}\epsilon(e_i)e_i=e_i$, and both coassociative composites give $w_i^{-2}e_i\otimes e_i\otimes e_i$. On a basis tensor $e_i\otimes e_j$, each of the two Frobenius composites and $\Delta\mu$ equals $0$ if $i\ne j$ and equals $w_i^{-1}e_i\otimes e_i$ if $i=j$. By bilinearity the counit, coassociativity, and Frobenius identities hold on all inputs, so these maps form a commutative Frobenius algebra.

Apply [F1] to the finite-dimensional commutative Frobenius algebra established in steps 1.1–1.2. The resulting functor has the genus-$g$ evaluation and cylinder action stated in the Definition by [F2]; no positivity or open-sector hypothesis is used.

citations.quote: Fix an integer $r\ge1$ and let $A=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{r}\mathbb C e_i$, with coordinatewise multiplication $e_i e_j=\delta_{ij}e_i$ and unit $1_A=\sum_{i=1}^{r}e_i$. Choose weights $w_i\in\mathbb C^\times$ and define $\epsilon(e_i)=w_i$ and $\Delta(e_i)=w_i^{-1}e_i\otimes e_i$.
For the connected closed surface $\Sigma_g$ of genus $g\ge0$, it assigns $Z_A(\Sigma_g)=\epsilon(H^g(\eta(1)))$; the cylinder acts by $1_A$.

derivations.claim: Since $\eta(1)=\sum_i e_i$, repeated application of the diagonal action in step 1.1 gives $H^g(\eta(1))=\sum_i w_i^{-g}e_i$ for each integer $g\ge0$; at $g=0$ this is the identity convention in [F2].

Apply $\epsilon$ and use $\epsilon(e_i)=w_i$ to obtain $Z_A(\Sigma_g)=\epsilon(H^g(\eta(1)))=\sum_i w_i^{1-g}$. The cylinder is $1_A$ by [F2], and for $g=1$ every summand is $1$, so the torus amplitude is $r$.

At g=1, w_i^(1-g)=1 for every i, so step 3.1 yields r.

The supplied closed classification associates to $(A,\mu,\eta,\Delta,\epsilon)$ a closed oriented two-dimensional TQFT.

derivations.claim: If $a=\sum_i a_i e_i$ and $b=\sum_i b_i e_i$, then $a^*b=\sum_i\overline{a_i}b_i e_i$, so $h(a,b)=\sum_i w_i\overline{a_i}b_i$.
If every $w_i$ is positive real, the formula in step 1.1 is Hermitian and $h(a,a)=\sum_i w_i|a_i|^2>0$ for each nonzero $a$, because at least one coefficient is nonzero.

Conversely, if $h$ is Hermitian and positive definite, then $w_i=h(e_i,e_i)$ is real by Hermitian symmetry and strictly positive by positive definiteness for every nonzero basis vector $e_i$. Thus all weights are positive real, proving the equivalence.

The classification used in [F2] assumes only the nonzero Frobenius weights, so the algebraic closed theory remains defined when the extra positivity condition fails; this separates the categorical model from the specified Hilbert-space interpretation.

citations.quote: For any field $k$, the category of strong symmetric monoidal functors $\mathsf{Cob}^{\mathrm{cl}}_2\to\mathrm{Vect}_{\mathrm{fd}}(k)$ and monoidal natural transformations is equivalent to the category of finite-dimensional commutative Frobenius $k$-algebras and maps preserving multiplication, unit, comultiplication, and counit.

derivations.claim: Every class in $A$ is uniquely $a+bx$ with $a,b\in\mathbb C$, and $(a+bx)(c+dx)=ac+(ad+bc)x$ because $x^2=0$. This is the quotient of the associative commutative algebra $\mathbb C[x]$, so $A$ is a two-dimensional commutative unital associative algebra with nonzero nilpotent $x$.
The pairing values are $b(1,1)=0$, $b(1,x)=1$, $b(x,1)=1$, and $b(x,x)=0$, so its matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ and determinant $-1\ne0$. Hence $b$ is nondegenerate.

Define $\Delta(1)=1\otimes x+x\otimes1$ and $\Delta(x)=x\otimes x$. On both basis elements, $(\epsilon\otimes1)\Delta=(1\otimes\epsilon)\Delta=\operatorname{id}_A$ as counit identities; the two coassociative composites on $1$ both equal $1\otimes x\otimes x+x\otimes1\otimes x+x\otimes x\otimes1$, and on $x$ both equal $x\otimes x\otimes x$. For the two Frobenius identities, bilinearity reduces to the four basis pairs $(1,1),(1,x),(x,1),(x,x)$; on these pairs all three composites $\Delta\mu$, $(1\otimes\mu)(\Delta\otimes1)$, and $(\mu\otimes1)(1\otimes\Delta)$ respectively equal $\Delta(1),\Delta(x),\Delta(x),0$. Thus the specified maps make $A$ a commutative Frobenius algebra.

The ideal $(x)$ is maximal because $A/(x)\cong\mathbb C$. For every maximal ideal $M$, the quotient $A/M$ is a field and the image of $x$ there is nilpotent because $x^2=0$; a field has no nonzero nilpotents, so $x\in M$. Hence $0\ne x\in J(A)$, the intersection of all maximal left ideals, and $A$ is not semisimple under the stated definition.

For $a=a_0+a_1x$ and $b=b_0+b_1x$, $h(a,b)=\overline{a_0}b_1+\overline{a_1}b_0$, so $h(a,b)=\overline{h(b,a)}$ and the form is Hermitian. Also $h(1+x,1+x)=\epsilon((1+x)^2)=2$ while $h(1-x,1-x)=\epsilon((1-x)^2)=-2$, so it takes both signs and is not positive definite.

By step 2.1 the algebra is finite-dimensional, commutative, and Frobenius, so [F1] applies over $k=\mathbb C$ and gives the closed oriented two-dimensional TQFT. This conclusion uses the closed category only and adds no open/closed or positivity claim.
